content: Testing for hepatitis in areas with limited access to healthcare or poor linkage to care and treatment provides minimal benefit to affected individuals. For hepatitis B and C serosurveys, pre-test information will be shared with households only after obtaining their consent to participate. This information should be clear and concise, covering the following points: 1. Two tests will be conducted: one for hepatitis B and one for hepatitis C.g., via contaminated needles) or body fluids. However, they cannot be spread through casual contact, such as shaking hands or sharing food. 2. Hepatitis B and C are chronic diseases that can silently damage the liver over time, potentially leading to scarring, liver cancer, or death. Hepatitis B is preventable with a vaccine, requiring three doses for full protection. 3. Test results will be confidential and shared only with the individual tested. The tests detect the presence of the virus in the blood: A negative result indicates no virus is present. A positive result means the virus is present, posing a long-term risk of liver complications. In such cases, steps can be taken to reduce the risk of complications, and treatment or follow-up may be necessary. Post-test counseling will be tailored to each individual’s situation. For those testing positive for hepatitis B: The presence of the virus in the blood suggests potential long-term liver damage. Additional tests will be needed to assess the viral load and liver damage. It is recommended that they be vaccinated against hepatitis B and tested for past infection. To protect the liver, alcohol consumption may need to be reduced, and maintaining a healthy weight through proper diet and regular physical activity is encouraged. If there is a regular sexual partner, discussing the situation with them is advised so they can get vaccinated. Assistance can be provided for this process. For those testing positive for hepatitis C: The virus may still be present and harmful to the liver, or it may have resolved on its own. Further testing is required to confirm the presence of the virus and assess liver damage. Close contacts should be tested for past infection, as no vaccine is available for hepatitis C. To prevent liver damage, alcohol consumption may need to be limited, and a healthy lifestyle is encouraged. Conversations with sexual partners about the situation can be considered, though the risk of sexual transmission is very low. For individuals testing negative, results will not be actively communicated unless they contact the testing center with their identification number and answer a security question. No counseling will be provided for these individuals. Families of children will already have been advised to complete the hepatitis B vaccine series if not already done. Additional referrals may be provided for prevention, counseling, and support services, including HIV, tuberculosis, sexually transmitted infections, contraception, antenatal care, alcohol reduction, opioid substitution therapy, access to sterile needles, and safe-sex counseling, as appropriate.
